description: Hi! I’m Maya, a high school student ,interested in sustainability, technology, science, and creative problem-solving. I’m a co-founder of CYCLE, a plastic-waste initiative connecting discarded plastic with initiatives and companies that can reuse it. We are looking for curious teammates skilled in web development, data analysis, environmental science . Let’s build real projects!
summary: Cycle is a working web platform that connects two things the plastic problem keeps apart: the plastic on the ground and the satellite evidence about the place it sits in. People photograph, classify and post recyclable plastic; verified recyclers and plants publish the material they need; the platform matches the two, records the hand-off and turns every collection into an environmental figure. Alongside it, an Earth Intelligence Engine reads open NASA MODIS data for seven Egyptian zones and any coordinate on Earth, and reports vegetation, surface-temperature and land-cover trends with quality flags, sample counts and 95% confidence intervals, stating openly when a record is too short to support a conclusion. Each zone ends in a plain-language change story and a recommended local action. For the "Be An Earth System Trend Detective" challenge this matters because a trend is only useful if someone can act on it: Cycle turns a defensible satellite signal into a decision about material that is physically there. The platform is live and fully functional; the listings and impact figures currently on it are demonstration data.
details: What Cycle does. Cycle is a working web platform with two connected layers. The community layer turns recyclable plastic into a published, searchable listing and matches it with industrial demand. The Earth layer is an Earth Intelligence Engine that reads open NASA satellite products for an area, separates a real trend from year-to-year noise, states how confident it is, and translates the result into a local action. The two layers meet on the same zone page, which is the core idea: a satellite trend gets a physical counterpart, and a material flow gets environmental context. How it works, main task A — try this one. Open https://cycle-studio.ai.studio, go to Plastic Reports and filter by polymer and status to see posted material. Then open Organization Needs: each open requirement shows how many published reports match it and the best match score. Open the requirement, compare the matching listing, and the hand-off is recorded as collected. Every completed hand-off is converted on impactMetrics into weight diverted, CO₂e avoided, landfill volume avoided and energy conserved. A person reporting plastic goes through Report Plastic Waste: photo, polymer, estimated weight, location. How it works, main task B. Open Earth Intelligence and choose one of seven Egyptian case-study zones, or type any latitude and longitude. The engine retrieves the matching MODIS products for that area and shows four indicator cards: vegetation index, day and night land-surface temperature, land-cover class, and local Cycle supply. The map tab compares NASA GIBS imagery for a chosen date with Cycle pins on top. Vegetation Trends gives the NDVI and EVI slope per year, its 95% confidence interval, the baseline anomaly and how many composites passed the quality filter, with a standard and a strict filter. Thermal and Land Cover shows day and night temperature curves and land-cover composition. The Change Story tab explains the result in plain language and recommends an action; the export panel produces a GeoTIFF or NetCDF4 request through AppEEARS. Benefits. Households and small businesses get a direct route for sorted plastic. Recyclers get a ranked demand board instead of phone calls. Municipalities, journalists and students get a defensible reading of vegetation, heat and land-cover change for a district, with the caveats printed next to the numbers. Researchers get quality-filtered data they can export and repeat. Goals. Near term, prove a repeatable loop in one district: material collected, matched and counted, alongside a satellite record that shows the context. Medium term, onboard verified organizations with an audit trail and let municipalities use the zone page in planning. Long term, a decision layer where a visible environmental trend and the material flow that feeds it are read together, in any city, on open data. Tools, languages and hardware. HTML, CSS and JavaScript single-page application with client-side routing and a full Arabic/English right-to-left interface; Leaflet with NASA GIBS WMTS tiles and OpenStreetMap base data; charting for the vegetation and temperature time series; NASA AppEEARS for product subsetting; MODIS MOD13Q1, MOD11A2 and MCD12Q1 (Collection 6.1) as the measurements; Git and GitHub for version control; Google AI Studio for deployment and hosting; FFmpeg for assembling the demo video. Hardware: ordinary laptops. No sensors, no field equipment and no paid data subscriptions. What works now. Reporting, listing, search and filtering; organization demand publishing; matching with match score; collection status; impact accounting; individual and organization accounts; the bilingual interface; and the whole Earth Intelligence layer — seven zones, global coordinate query, four indicator cards, GIBS map explorer with date and opacity controls, vegetation trends with quality filters, thermal and land-cover analysis, change stories, export panel and a provenance and limits panel. What is not finished. The community layer runs on demonstration data: every listing, organization, need and figure currently displayed is seeded sample data, not a field result. The Egyptian zones carry less than five years of MODIS record, so long-term trends are labelled exploratory and no decadal projection is offered. MCD12Q1 is annual at 500 m, so narrow urban strips can be misclassified as barren; the interface says so next to the percentages. GIBS imagery is a visual aid only and is never used for a quantitative claim. There is no pickup scheduling engine yet, and organization verification is manual, without an automated audit trail. What we plan to add. A verified onboarding flow with an audit trail; pickup scheduling and confirmation inside the application; alerts when a zone slope or anomaly crosses a threshold; one-click PDF and CSV impact statements for municipal partners and sponsors; saved areas beyond the pre-loaded Egyptian zones; and evaluation of further NASA products, such as rainfall or soil moisture, under the same quality-first discipline.
